In [[mathematics]], the '''Frobenius determinant theorem''' states that if one takes the [[multiplication table]] of a finite [[Group (mathematics)|group]] ''G'' and replaces each entry ''g'' with a variable ''x''<sub>''g''</sub>, and subsequently takes the [[determinant]], then the resulting multivariable polynomial factors as a product of ''n'' irreducible polynomials, where ''n'' is the number of [[conjugacy classes]] of ''G''. Moreover, in the factorization, each of these irreducibles appears raised to a power equal to its degree.

This was first stated as a conjecture in a letter of 1896 by the mathematician [[Richard Dedekind]] to [[Ferdinand Georg Frobenius|F. G. Frobenius]], who proved it by methods which began a new branch of mathematics, the [[representation theory of finite groups]].<ref>{{harvnb|Etingof|2005|p=1}}</ref> See {{harv|Dedekind|1968}}, with English translation {{harv|Curtis|2003|loc=p.&nbsp;51}}.

==Formal statement==
Let a [[finite group]] <math>G</math> have elements <math>g_1, g_2,\dots,g_n</math>, and let <math>x_{g_i}</math> be associated with each element of <math>G</math>. Define the matrix <math>X_G</math> with entries <math>a_{ij}=x_{g_i g_j}</math>. Then:

: <math> \det X_G = \prod_{j=1}^r P_j(x_{g_1},x_{g_2},\dots,x_{g_n})^{\deg P_j}</math>

where the <math>P_{j}</math>'s are pairwise non-proportional irreducible polynomials and <math>r</math> is the number of conjugacy classes of&nbsp;''G''.<ref>{{harvnb|Etingof|2005|loc=Theorem 5.4.}}</ref>

==Examples==
If <math>G=\Z/2\Z=\{e,g\}</math> with <math>g^2=e</math> with ''n ='' 2 conjugacy classes, the matrix would be:

:<math>X_G = \begin{bmatrix} x_{e} & x_g \\ x_g & x_{e} \end{bmatrix}.</math>

The determinant of this matrix has ''n ='' 2 [[irreducible polynomial|irreducible]] factors of degree 1, each with multiplicity 1:

:<math>\det X_G = (x_e - x_g)(x_e + x_g).</math>

If <math>G=S_3</math>, the [[symmetric group]] of order 3, the matrix would be:

:<math>X_G = \begin{bmatrix}
x_{e} & x_{(12)} & x_{(23)} & x_{(31)} & x_{(123)} & x_{(321)}\\
x_{(12)} & x_{e} & x_{(321)} & x_{(123)} & x_{(31)} & x_{(23)}\\
x_{(23)} & x_{(123)} & x_{e} & x_{(321)} & x_{(12)} & x_{(31)}\\
x_{(31)} &  x_{(321)} & x_{(123)} & x_{e} & x_{(23)} & x_{(12)}\\
x_{(123)} & x_{(23)} & x_{(31)} & x_{(12)} & x_{(321)} & x_{e}\\
x_{(321)} & x_{(31)} & x_{(12)} & x_{(23)} & x_{e} & x_{(123)}
\end{bmatrix}.</math>

The determinant of this matrix factors out as:

:<math>\textstyle \det X_G = \left(\sum_{\sigma\in S_3}x_\sigma\right)
\left(\sum_{\sigma\in S_3}\text{sign}(\sigma)x_\sigma\right)
\left(F(x_{e},x_{(123)},x_{(321)})-F(x_{(12)},x_{(23)},x_{(31)})\right)^2</math>

where <math>F(a,b,c)=a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca</math>. The number of irreducible polynomial factors is three, which is equal to the number of conjugacy classes of <math>S_3</math>. The degree-2 polynomial factor has multiplicity 2.<ref name="Chen">{{harvnb|Chen|loc=Chapter 22.}}</ref>

==Proof==

This proof is based on the one given by Evan Chen, which involves [[representation theory]].<ref name="Chen"/> It relies on the following lemma:

{{math theorem|name=Lemma|1=Let <math>Y</math> be an <math>n\times n</math> matrix whose entries are independent variables <math>y_{ij}</math>. Then <math>\det Y</math> is an irreducible polynomial.}}

Let <math>V=(V,\rho)=\C[G]</math> be the [[regular representation]] of group <math>G</math>. Consider the [[linear map]]:

:<math>T=\sum_{g\in G}x_g\rho(g)</math>,

whose matrix is given by <math>X_G</math>. We wish to examine <math>\det T</math>.

By [[Maschke's theorem]], <math>\C[G]</math> is a [[semisimple algebra]], so it is possible to break down <math>V</math> into a direct sum of [[irreducible representations]],

:<math>V=\bigoplus_{i=1}^rV_i^{\oplus\dim V_i}</math>

where each <math>V_i</math> is an irreducible representation of <math>V</math>. This lets us write:

:<math>\det T=\prod_{i=1}^r\left(\det(T|_{V_i})\right)^{\dim V_i},</math>

where each <math>\det(T|_{V_i})</math> is a polynomial factor of <math>\det T</math>.

A result from [[character theory]] states that the number of nonisomorphic irreps of regular representation <math>V</math> equals the number of [[conjugacy classes]] of <math>G</math>. This explains why the number of polynomial factors is equal to the number of conjugacy classes.

Furthermore, <math>\dim V_i</math> is both the degree and multiplicity of the polynomial <math>\det(T|_{V_i})</math>, which explains why the degree and multiplicity of each polynomial factor are equal.

To complete the proof, we wish to show that polynomials <math>\det(T|_{V_i})</math> are irreducible and not proportional to each other.

'''Proof of irreducibility''': By [[Jacobson density theorem]], for any matrix <math>M\in\text{Mat}(V_i)</math>, there exists a particular choice of complex numbers for each <math>x_g\in G</math> such that:
:<math>M=\sum_{g\in G}x_g\rho_i(g)=T|_{V_i}(\{x_g\})</math>
This shows that <math>T|_{V_i}</math>, when viewed as a matrix with polynomial entries, must have linearly independent entries. Thus, by letting each of these entries be an independent variable <math>y_{ij}</math>, it follows by Lemma above that <math>\det T|_{V_i}</math> is an irreducible polynomial.

'''Proof of non-proportionality''': This follows by noticing that we can read off the [[Character theory|character]] <math>\chi_{V_i}</math> from the coefficients of <math>\det T|_{V_i}</math>, using the fact that for all <math>g\in G</math>, the coefficient of <math>x_gx_{1_G}^{k-1}</math> in <math>\det T|_{V_i}</math> is equal to <math>\chi_{V_i}(g)</math>. Since characters are linearly independent to each other, it follows that <math>\det T|_{V_i}</math> is not proportional to any other polynomial factor.
